title: RMSProp Explained in Detail with Animations | Optimizers in Deep Learning Part 5
full_text: Hi guys, my name is Nitish and you are  welcome to my YouTube channel. In this  video too, we will continue our deep  learning playlist. We are studying  optimizers in deep learning. And the  next optimizer we are going to study is  named RMSprop. So, let's start the  video. Let's start our discussion  around RMSprop. Okay? First of all,  let's look at its full form. The full  form of RMSprop is Root Mean Square.  Prop. Okay, and this optimization  technique is basically an improvement  over Adagrad. So, if you want to  understand Root Mean Square Prop, you  must have knowledge of Adagrad. Whose  video I shared in the last video.  Although, I will give you a few details . So, what did we discuss in the last  video? That you use Adagrad when you  have sparse data. Sparse data means  that in some of your columns, suppose a  lot of values are zero. So, you call  this type of data sparse. So, what  happens with sparse data is that the  contour plot of your loss function with  respect to parameters becomes very  elongated. It becomes like this. Like  this, as you can see here. Now, what is  the problem with this? That when you  try to optimize and reach the minima,  you come by making movements like this.  Okay? Which wastes time. Ideally, there  should be a movement like this,  directly to this spot. So, I showed you  through animations how your Batch  Gradient Descent or Momentum, both  optimize over these stretched curves  through these movements, which are  time-consuming and slow. So, this is  where Adagrad came in, and what did  Adagrad do? It solved this problem.  Right? Now, we also discussed that  Adagrad had a very big disadvantage.  And that disadvantage was that in  Adagrad, you do what? You reduce the  learning rate. You reduce it. But after  a point, the learning rate reduces so  much that the update becomes very small . Due to which, what happens is that  your Adagrad algorithm is unable to  converge properly. If this is the  minima, it will come here and stop. It  will come here and stop. It cannot make  this movement. Because you have reduced  the learning rate so much that the  updates being made are very, very small  and it gets stuck at one place. So,  this was the biggest problem with  Adagrad. RMSprop solves exactly this  problem. Right? So we will try to  understand the mathematics behind it  and then look at how this whole thing  works through an animation. Let’s  look at the problem I mentioned earlier  in AdaGrad mathematically. So, we have  data where one column consists only of  ones. In one column, we have our  x-values which contain many sparse  values. And then, we have our output  column y. Corresponding to this column,  we have parameter B. Corresponding to X , we have parameter M. So, when you  plot the graph, since X or you could  say M is sparse, an elongated bowl  problem occurs. Now, as I told you in  the last video about AdaGrad, what  happens is that you move rapidly in the  direction of B first, and then you move  in the direction of M. Meaning,  initially, you are making changes in B.  Because it is non-sparse. And then,  after a point, you start changing in  the direction of M. But sometimes,  suppose this is your local minima, you  end up stopping right here at this spot . You are unable to cover this distance . Meaning, you are unable to move back  in B. The reason is that B is your  non-sparse parameter. Now, what is  happening here? Mathematically, if you  look, you are dividing the learning  rate of B by this number VT. And what  is VT? The sum of squares of all past  gradients. So, after many epochs, you  will keep adding all the gradients from  the start up to that epoch, making this  number very large. As soon as this  number becomes large, the learning rate  for B becomes very small. And that is  why you cannot take a movement in this  direction. You will stop right here. I  hope you understand the problem. So,  the entire issue originates solely from  the fact that when calculating this vt  term, you are considering all past  gradients, which causes vt to become  very large. Because of that, this whole  term becomes very small, and the update  becomes negligible. So we have to stop  this vt from becoming too large in some  way, and that is exactly the problem  RMSprop solves. Let me show it to you.  In RMSprop, you make a small change,  and that small change is that you use  this formula while calculating vt. Beta  times vt-1 + 1-beta times the square of  the gradient, and the formula below  remains exactly the same. Where beta is  generally taken to be 0.95. Alright?  You can change it as well. So what is  the main difference? Previously, you  were taking the entire history of your  gradients right from the first epoch.  Now, what you are doing is taking an  exponentially weighted average. You are  taking an exponentially decaying  average. Where you are giving more  weight to the recent gradients and not  much weight to the values from older  epochs. So, automatically, this vt term  will not become as large as it was  becoming here. Because of that, the  learning rate won't become too small,  and the whole term won't shrink too  much, so you will continue to get  updates. We can also prove this  mathematically. You can see, if you  assume v0 is 0, then what will v1 be?  .95 multiplied by 0, because vt-1 is 0,  plus .05 times the square of the  gradient in step or epoch one. Then we  calculated v2, so v2 will be this plus  this. Then we calculated v3, so v3 will  be this plus this plus this. You can  see as we move forward, this gradient  is for epoch one. This is what came in  epoch two, and this is epoch three,  which is the most recent epoch. You can  see that the value from epoch one is  being multiplied by so many numbers.  And since these numbers are less than  one, it becomes an even smaller number.  Whereas this will be the largest one.  So, what we said earlier, that you give  the most value to the most recent  epochs and kind of start forgetting the  older epochs. That is why I wrote here  that this is an exponentially decaying  average. Right? And because of this, vt  never shoots up. It does not become  very large. Which prevents the learning  rate from becoming too small, and  updates keep happening. Because of this , the problem in Adagrad does not stop  here. It converges. Right? Let me show  you through an animation. Although you  won't see any difference in the  animation. In AdaGrad and RMSProp.  Because I told you in the last video  that you see this problem with AdaGrad  when you are working with complex  neural networks, or it can be said when  you are doing non-convex optimization.  AdaGrad works perfectly fine in the  case of convex optimization problems  like linear regression. And this entire  animation I have created, in fact, all  these graphs you see, are based on a  linear regression problem. That is why  you will see here that AdaGrad is  converging towards the global minima.  But if you apply AdaGrad to a proper  neural network, you would see that it  is unable to reach the global minima.  But RMSProp does. In both places,  whether you are applying it to linear  regression or to a neural network. So  you can see, this is RMSProp. We have  applied it to the same problem and you  can see its trajectory is very similar  to AdaGrad. In fact, I will show you  side by side. This is AdaGrad, and you  would notice its trajectory is exactly  like RMSProp. Because this is a convex  optimization problem. We have worked on  a linear regression problem. And that  is why both algorithms are behaving  exactly similarly. But if you work on a  non-convex optimization problem. If you  work on some complex neural network.  You would see that AdaGrad will not be  able to reach the minima. Whereas  RMSProp reaches it. Okay? So, I won't  be able to show you much through  animations here. But you have to  understand what the benefits are. Now  the question is, does RMSProp also have  any disadvantages? The answer is no. It  is empirically proven that RMSProp is  one of the best optimization techniques  to optimize neural networks. In fact,  before Adam came along, we mostly used  RMSProp to optimize our neural networks . So RMSProp still competes with Adam  today. If you don't get good enough  results from Adam in some problem, you  still use RMSProp. Okay? So as such,  there is no disadvantage here. It's  just that Adam is a technique that came  along and started performing a bit  better than RMSProp, which is why  RMSProp is used a little less. But it  is still a very, very powerful  optimization technique which has no  disadvantages. So that was the video,  guys. I hope you understood the video.  If you liked the video, please like it,  and if you haven't subscribed to the  channel, please subscribe. That's it  from my side. See you in the next video . Bye.
